title: Docker Security Best Practices
description: Harden container images with security scanning, least privilege, and image signing.

data.text: Containers share the host kernel, which means a vulnerability in one container can potentially affect the entire host and other containers running on it. Securing containers involves multiple layers: the image content, the build pipeline, the runtime environment, and the supply chain that delivers images.

terms.definition: The process of analyzing container images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in the base image and installed packages.
Running containers with the minimum permissions necessary, avoiding root or privileged mode.
A Docker feature that ensures images are signed by trusted publishers before they can be pulled.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a shared list of publicly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

data.title: Secure Dockerfile practices
data.content: A Dockerfile that follows security best practices: minimal base, specific user, small attack surface.
data.code:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0-jammy-chiseled-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup app/ .

USER appuser

EXPOSE 80
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "MyApp.dll"]

data.title: Use distroless or alpine images
data.text: Distroless and Alpine-based images contain only your application and its dependencies — no package manager, shell, or other binaries. This dramatically reduces the attack surface.

cards.title: Full OS image (e.g., ubuntu)
cards.description: Contains a full Linux distribution with package manager and many binaries.

cards.title: Distroless (e.g., gcr.io/distroless)
cards.description: Contains only your application — no shell, package manager, or OS tools.

data.text: Image scanners check your container images against databases of known vulnerabilities. They scan every layer of the image — including the base image, installed packages, and application dependencies.

data.title: Scanning with Trivy
data.content: Install Trivy and scan a container image for vulnerabilities.
data.code:
# Install Trivy
brew install aquasecurity/trivy/trivy

# Scan a local image
trive image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myapp:latest

# Scan in CI (GitHub Actions)
- name: Scan image
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: 'myapp:${{ github.sha }}'
    severity: 'HIGH,CRITICAL'
    exit-code: '1'

data.text: **Docker Content Trust** (DCT) uses Notary to sign and verify image publishers. When enabled, you can only pull images that have been signed by trusted authorities. Similarly, you should pin images to specific digests rather than tags to guarantee the exact image you tested is what runs in production.

data.title: Enabling Docker Content Trust
data.content: Set the environment variable to enable image signing verification.
data.code:
# Enable content trust
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1

# Sign an image during push
docker trust sign myapp:latest

# Verify signatures
 docker trust inspect myapp:latest

data.title: Pin by digest, not tag
data.text: Tags can be overwritten after you've tested them. Always reference production images by their digest (e.g., `myapp@sha256:abc123...`) to ensure immutability.

data.caption: The container security lifecycle: build securely, scan early, sign, and verify at runtime.
data.definition:
graph TB
    A[Build with secure Dockerfile] --> B[Scan for CVEs]
    B --> C[Sign image]

    D --> E[Deploy to cluster]
    E --> F[Runtime monitoring]

data.title: Harden a container image
data.description: Apply security best practices to an existing image.
steps: Review your Dockerfile: is it using a minimal base image?
Add a non-root USER to the Dockerfile.
Create a .dockerignore file to exclude sensitive files.
Scan the image with Trivy: `trivy image myapp:latest`.
Fix any HIGH or CRITICAL findings.
data.expectedOutcome: A hardened container image with no critical vulnerabilities and a non-root user.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Start from minimal base images (distroless, Alpine) to reduce attack surface.
Never run containers as root — always create and use a non-root user.
Scan images for CVEs in CI before pushing to a registry.
Pin images by digest and enable Docker Content Trust for supply chain security.
Security is a lifecycle — secure the build, scan during CI, and monitor at runtime.
data.takeaway: Container security is not optional — bake it into your build pipeline from day one.
